recipes.title: Know where you are
recipes.explanation: Print your current directory before running project commands. Relative paths start here.

recipes.title: Find what a command really is
recipes.explanation: Shows aliases, functions and every executable match, in the order zsh would pick them. This is how you discover that ls is really an alias for eza.

recipes.title: Read your PATH
recipes.explanation: zsh exposes PATH as an array. The first matching executable wins.

recipes.title: Learn the command you already have
recipes.explanation: Local manuals match the installed operating system. Press / to search and q to quit.

recipes.title: Inspect an alias
recipes.explanation: gs expands to git status. Run alias with no arguments to list aliases.

recipes.title: Inspect a shell function
recipes.explanation: Read a function's implementation before relying on it. Run functions with no arguments to list every function your shell has defined.

recipes.title: Look up recent commands
recipes.explanation: Read the last 20 history entries. Ctrl+R opens your fuzzy history picker.

recipes.title: Quote paths with spaces
recipes.explanation: Double quotes preserve spaces and expand variables. Single quotes preserve literal text.

recipes.title: Capture command output
recipes.explanation: Command substitution captures stdout. Use this inside a Git repository.

recipes.title: Act only after success
recipes.explanation: && runs the second command only if the first exits successfully. Run in a project with both scripts.

recipes.title: Count tracked source files
recipes.explanation: Count or inspect tracked files without searching node_modules. Add a pipe to wc -l for the count.

recipes.title: Write output without clobbering
recipes.explanation: If you have set NO_CLOBBER (setopt noclobber), > refuses to replace an existing file. Use a fresh filename.

recipes.title: Append a line
recipes.explanation: >> appends. Use >| only when you deliberately want to overwrite despite NO_CLOBBER.

recipes.title: Keep spaces safe when iterating
recipes.command: for file in *.md(N); do print -r -- "$file"; done
recipes.explanation: (N) makes an unmatched zsh glob expand to nothing. Quote the variable on use.

recipes.title: See shell jobs
recipes.explanation: Ctrl+Z suspends a foreground job; fg resumes it. Ctrl+C asks the foreground process to stop.

recipes.title: Resume a suspended job
recipes.explanation: Return the most recently suspended shell job to the foreground.

recipes.title: Check shell syntax
recipes.explanation: Parse the config without executing it. This catches syntax errors, not every runtime problem.

recipes.title: Start a clean shell
recipes.explanation: Start a shell without your normal startup files. Type exit to leave. Useful for isolating config bugs.

recipes.title: Show completion paths
recipes.explanation: These directories contain completion functions, including Homebrew's site-functions directory.

recipes.title: Open this handbook
recipes.explanation: Opens the handbook in your browser. It is a single file and works offline. On Linux, use xdg-open index.html.

recipes.title: Build a pipeline
recipes.explanation: Send stdout from Git into wc. This counts tracked TypeScript files, avoiding dependency folders.

recipes.title: Understand pipe failures
recipes.explanation: The subshell keeps the setting local. Without pipefail, cat can succeed and hide the failure from false. After a pipeline, print -l -- $pipestatus shows each stage.

recipes.title: Save a jump as an alias
recipes.explanation: An alias is a saved command. Add the line to your .zshrc to keep it after this session, then open a new shell.

recipes.title: Jump by remembered name
recipes.explanation: zoxide learns visited directories. zi opens an interactive picker. Visit the directory with cd first if it is unknown.

recipes.title: See files with Git status
recipes.explanation: A detailed directory listing. Your ll alias does the same with icons always enabled.

recipes.title: Explore a small tree
recipes.explanation: Keep output shallow. --git-ignore removes entries ignored by Git.

recipes.title: Find files by name
recipes.explanation: fd respects ignore files by default. It searches names, while rg searches file contents.

recipes.title: Find hidden config files
recipes.explanation: Lists names only; avoids printing secrets stored inside environment files.

recipes.title: Find directories
recipes.explanation: Narrow by type to locate component directories quickly.

recipes.title: Find text in source
recipes.explanation: Show line numbers for matching source files. Quoting prevents the shell from interpreting the pattern.

recipes.title: Search literal punctuation
recipes.explanation: -F treats the pattern as literal text, rather than a regular expression.

recipes.title: List matching files only
recipes.explanation: Useful before opening files in your editor. -l prints each matching filename once.

recipes.title: Count matches
recipes.explanation: Counts matching lines per file. Use --count-matches to count individual matches instead.

recipes.title: Search an ignored file deliberately
recipes.explanation: Replace the example path and pattern. Scope this tightly; searching every dependency is usually noise.

recipes.title: Choose a file interactively
recipes.explanation: Your fd default feeds ignored-aware file names into fzf. Ctrl+T inserts a selected path into the current command.

recipes.title: Jump with a directory picker
recipes.explanation: Interactive zoxide selector for directories you have already visited. Alt+C is fzf's directory picker.

recipes.title: Inspect file with highlighting
recipes.explanation: bat adds highlighting. ccat is your alias; ordinary cat remains available for scripts.

recipes.title: Read just part of a file
recipes.explanation: Useful when reviewing a large source file or config.

recipes.title: Plain portable directory tree
recipes.explanation: tree is also installed. The exclusion expression prevents huge dependency listings.

recipes.title: Count your codebase
recipes.explanation: Shows source line counts by language. Size is a navigation aid, not a quality score.

recipes.title: Understand current changes
recipes.explanation: Your gss alias gives short status; gs gives the detailed version.

recipes.title: Review unstaged changes
recipes.explanation: delta is already your configured pager. q exits; n and N navigate files when navigation is active.

recipes.title: Review what will be committed
recipes.explanation: Always check staged content before committing. gds is your alias.

recipes.title: Stage only intended hunks
recipes.explanation: Review and select individual changes. Type ? at a hunk prompt for the available choices.

recipes.title: Make a focused commit
recipes.explanation: Commit the staged changes with a concrete message. Replace the example message.

recipes.title: Start a feature branch
recipes.explanation: Creates and switches to a branch. Choose a name appropriate to the actual change.

recipes.title: See recent history
recipes.explanation: Your glog alias shows a similar graph. A compact history helps before a rebase or merge.

recipes.title: Fetch remote changes
recipes.explanation: Updates remote-tracking refs and prunes stale ones. It does not merge into your working branch.

recipes.title: Understand upstream differences
recipes.explanation: Requires a configured upstream. Left entries are local-only; right entries are upstream-only.

recipes.title: Unstage without losing edits
recipes.explanation: Replace the example path. This changes the index and preserves working-tree content.

recipes.title: Discard a file's local edits
recipes.explanation: Replaces uncommitted working-tree content. Inspect git diff first; ordinary Git may not recover these edits.

recipes.title: Find when a line changed
recipes.explanation: Replace the path. Follow up with git show COMMIT to understand the reason for a change.

recipes.title: Search the history of a string
recipes.explanation: Finds commits that change the number of occurrences of the string. Use -G for regex diff matching.

recipes.title: Recover a moved branch tip
recipes.explanation: Read recent ref movements before trying recovery. Create a rescue branch from the desired commit.

recipes.title: Create a parallel checkout
recipes.explanation: Adds a separate checkout and new branch without disturbing current work. Run inside the intended repo.

recipes.title: List parallel checkouts
recipes.explanation: Useful when reviewing work while a development server runs in another checkout.

recipes.title: Check whitespace errors
recipes.explanation: Detects whitespace problems and conflict markers in changes.

recipes.title: Use a Git dashboard
recipes.explanation: Interactive status, hunk staging, history and branches. Read on-screen bindings before performing actions.

recipes.title: Inspect large-file tracking
recipes.explanation: Lists files tracked by Git LFS. LFS stores pointers in Git and file content separately.

recipes.title: Check GitHub login
recipes.explanation: Reports authentication status without requesting token output.

recipes.title: List your pull requests
recipes.explanation: Run in the relevant GitHub repository.

recipes.title: Review a pull request locally
recipes.explanation: Replace 123 with a real PR number; prints its patch.

recipes.title: Check CI for a PR
recipes.explanation: Shows check status. Use gh run list to explore recent workflow runs.

recipes.title: Inspect failed CI logs
recipes.explanation: Replace RUN_ID with a real run ID from gh run list. Logs may contain sensitive project details.

recipes.title: Create a draft PR
recipes.explanation: Opens an interactive draft-PR flow and sends content to GitHub. Review title, body and target branch.

recipes.title: Check runtime selection
recipes.explanation: Shows the default Node and the tools Volta manages. Without Volta, use node --version and which -a node.

recipes.title: See the actual Node binary
recipes.explanation: Shows the executable Volta would select in the current project.

recipes.title: List project scripts
recipes.explanation: With no script, pnpm lists the scripts declared in package.json. Use this before assuming test or dev exists.

recipes.title: Install the locked dependencies
recipes.explanation: Run in a pnpm project with a current lockfile. Refuses changes to the lockfile; installs dependencies.

recipes.title: Start a development server
recipes.explanation: Starts the project's dev script. Databases and environment variables still need to be available. Ctrl+C stops it.

recipes.title: Match the project's package manager
recipes.explanation: The lockfile tells you which package manager the project uses. Mixing them produces inconsistent installs.

recipes.title: Check types
recipes.explanation: Runs TypeScript without emitting JavaScript, if the project declares the script. pnpm run lists what exists.

recipes.title: Lint project code
recipes.explanation: Runs the project's linter. Fix the underlying issue rather than suppressing the rule globally.

recipes.title: Build for production
recipes.explanation: Runs the project's build, writing output such as .next. A build can require services and environment variables.

recipes.title: Run unit tests
recipes.explanation: Executes the project's test script. Read package.json to see which runner it uses.

recipes.title: Run browser tests
recipes.explanation: Runs end-to-end tests where the project declares them. Browsers, test data and a running server usually have to be set up first.

recipes.title: Explain a dependency
recipes.explanation: Find which dependency brings a package into the graph. Better than adding duplicate global packages.

recipes.title: Inspect direct versions
recipes.explanation: Lists top-level packages in the current project.

recipes.title: Inspect outdated dependencies
recipes.explanation: Read the available versions before choosing an upgrade. A nonzero exit can indicate outdated packages.

recipes.title: Use a project executable
recipes.explanation: Runs the locally installed executable. It does not install a new CLI like pnpm dlx may do.

recipes.title: Pin Node intentionally
recipes.explanation: Writes a Volta pin into package.json so everyone on the project gets that Node. Agree on it with the repository first.

recipes.title: Run any declared script
recipes.explanation: Replace build:types with a script from pnpm run. Generated output is written into the project.

recipes.title: Inspect npm globals
recipes.explanation: A diagnostic inventory. Keep application dependencies in their projects.

recipes.title: Check the VM (macOS)
recipes.explanation: On macOS, Docker needs a Linux VM. Colima reports its CPU, memory and mount settings. On Linux there is no VM: containers use the host kernel.

recipes.title: Check Docker's destination
recipes.explanation: Shows which engine your docker commands reach. A context name is not proof that anything is running.

recipes.title: List Docker contexts
recipes.explanation: Verify the target before running commands, especially if remote contexts are added later.

recipes.title: Start the container VM (macOS)
recipes.explanation: Starts the Colima profile. It does not start your project stacks. The Linux equivalent is sudo systemctl start docker.

recipes.title: Stop the container VM (macOS)
recipes.explanation: Stops every container in that VM. Useful when you want the memory back for something else; save running work first.

recipes.title: List running containers
recipes.explanation: Add -a to include stopped containers. Nothing running is a valid result.

recipes.title: See project service names
recipes.explanation: Run from the compose directory. Unlike full config output, this does not print interpolated environment secrets.

recipes.title: Validate Compose config
recipes.explanation: Checks the project's resolved configuration without printing it.

recipes.title: Start a WordPress site
recipes.explanation: Starts the project's services, downloading images and creating volumes if needed. The site's .env has to be configured first.

recipes.title: Check one site's status
recipes.explanation: Run from that site's directory.

recipes.title: Follow recent site logs
recipes.explanation: Ctrl+C leaves the log stream without stopping the containers. Logs can contain request details.

recipes.title: Check WordPress plugins
recipes.command: docker compose exec wpcli wp plugin list
recipes.explanation: Assumes the stack defines a wpcli service. Running WP-CLI in the container keeps the PHP and WordPress versions aligned with the site.

recipes.title: Check WordPress core
recipes.command: docker compose exec wpcli wp core version
recipes.explanation: Runs in the matching container environment, avoiding global PHP-version drift.

recipes.title: List WordPress options selectively
recipes.command: docker compose exec wpcli wp option get siteurl
recipes.explanation: Query one known option; avoid dumping all options, which can contain secrets.

recipes.title: Preview a URL migration
recipes.command: docker compose exec wpcli wp search-replace 'https://old.example' 'https://new.example' --all-tables-with-prefix --skip-columns=guid --dry-run
recipes.explanation: Replace the example URLs. Keep --dry-run until you have reviewed the result and backed up the database.

recipes.title: Export a WordPress database
recipes.command: docker compose exec wpcli wp db export db-seed/manual-backup.sql
recipes.explanation: Writes a potentially sensitive SQL backup to the mounted db-seed directory. Choose a new filename and keep it out of Git.

recipes.title: Stop a project, keep its data
recipes.explanation: Stops containers without removing them or volumes. up -d starts them again.

recipes.title: Remove stopped project containers
recipes.explanation: Removes project containers and networks. Do not add --volumes unless deliberately deleting database volumes.

recipes.title: Inspect Docker disk use
recipes.explanation: Reports images, containers, volumes and cache. Reclaimable volumes may still hold important databases.

recipes.title: Inspect live container resources
recipes.explanation: Takes a single CPU/memory snapshot of running containers.

recipes.title: Inspect image layers
recipes.explanation: Replace IMAGE:TAG with an image listed by docker image ls. Helps find oversized layers.

recipes.title: Lint a Dockerfile
recipes.explanation: Runs the installed Dockerfile linter on the local file.

recipes.title: Inspect the build engine
recipes.explanation: Lists builders and platforms before a multi-platform build.

recipes.title: Docker dashboard
recipes.explanation: Interactive container/log/resource UI. It includes actions that can stop or remove workloads.

recipes.title: Inspect Kubernetes context
recipes.explanation: Tells you which cluster the next kubectl command would hit. An error here usually means no kubeconfig, not a broken install.

recipes.title: Inspect Kubernetes workloads
recipes.explanation: Contacts the active cluster and lists pods in every namespace. Check the context before you run it.

recipes.title: List Helm releases
recipes.explanation: Read-only cluster query; requires a configured reachable Kubernetes cluster.

recipes.title: Kubernetes dashboard
recipes.explanation: Opens the read-only dashboard for the selected context.

recipes.title: List installed Python runtimes
recipes.explanation: A machine usually has several Pythons: the system one, a package-manager one and uv's. They are not interchangeable.

recipes.title: List isolated Python tools
recipes.explanation: Tools installed with uv tool install each get their own environment, so a CLI cannot break your projects.

recipes.title: Use a project's environment
recipes.explanation: In a uv project, respects the project's environment and Python requirements; may create or sync the environment.

recipes.title: Create a virtual environment
recipes.explanation: Creates .venv in the current directory. uv downloads that Python version if it is missing.

recipes.title: Activate a virtual environment
recipes.explanation: Run deactivate to leave. uv run avoids needing this at all, which is usually the better habit.

recipes.title: Sync a uv project
recipes.explanation: Uses the existing lockfile and fails if it needs updating. Run only in a uv project.

recipes.title: Run a Python script
recipes.explanation: Replace script.py with your actual script. Dependencies belong in the project.

recipes.title: Inspect dependency relationships
recipes.explanation: Prints the current project's dependency graph.

recipes.title: Add a declared dependency
recipes.explanation: Changes pyproject.toml, lockfile and environment. Use only when your project needs this dependency.

recipes.title: Find the Python interpreter
recipes.explanation: Use uv run python for the project-specific interpreter rather than assuming global python3 is the correct one.

recipes.title: Find the uv cache
recipes.explanation: Inspect before cleaning. uv cache prune is a separate mutation and cache cleanup means future downloads.

recipes.title: List local Ollama models
recipes.explanation: Shows downloaded models and their size on disk. Disk size is a rough floor for memory use, not a promise.

recipes.title: See loaded AI models
recipes.explanation: Shows models currently in memory. An empty list means the service is idle, not that Ollama is missing.

recipes.title: Run a model
recipes.explanation: Downloads the model on first use, then loads it into memory. Stop containers and other heavy work first on a small machine. /bye exits the chat.

recipes.title: Release a loaded model
recipes.explanation: Unloads the model from memory. It does not delete the downloaded files.

recipes.title: Inspect model metadata
recipes.explanation: Read the architecture, parameter count and context length before choosing settings.

recipes.title: Inspect llama.cpp options
recipes.explanation: Runs GGUF models directly, without a model manager. Start with conservative context sizes.

recipes.title: Run a local GGUF model
recipes.explanation: Replace the file path. Context size and GPU offload settings decide how much memory this takes.

recipes.title: Read a JSON field
recipes.explanation: Print just the scripts object. jq is for structured data; rg is for textual searching.

recipes.title: Get raw JSON text
recipes.explanation: -r outputs the string without JSON quotation marks.

recipes.title: Validate JSON
recipes.explanation: A successful exit confirms valid JSON; it does not validate an application-specific schema.

recipes.title: Browse large JSON interactively
recipes.explanation: Navigate structured data without printing a giant document. q quits.

recipes.title: Read Compose service names from YAML
recipes.explanation: Reads the raw YAML without Compose's variable interpolation. This is Mike Farah's Go yq, not the Python one.

recipes.title: Read Markdown nicely
recipes.explanation: Renders Markdown in the terminal. Helpful for project instructions.

recipes.title: Preview a text substitution
recipes.explanation: Transform piped text first to preview the result. Passing a filename to sd instead edits that file in place.

recipes.title: Edit a known string in one file
recipes.explanation: Replace placeholders; edits in place. Review git diff afterwards and use a narrow path.

recipes.title: Watch files and rerun tests
recipes.explanation: Runs tests after Python files change. Requires pytest in that project. Ctrl+C stops the watcher.

recipes.title: Benchmark two read-only commands
recipes.explanation: Example comparison of regex vs literal search. Run in a suitable repo; benchmark commands execute repeatedly.

recipes.title: Move a file to Trash
recipes.explanation: Sends the file to the desktop Trash instead of unlinking it, so you can get it back. On Linux the trash-cli command is usually trash-put.

recipes.title: Inspect an archive before extraction
recipes.explanation: libarchive's bsdtar reads zip, 7z, rar and more. Always read the filenames before extracting.

recipes.title: Extract into a fresh folder
recipes.explanation: Extracting into an empty directory stops a badly built archive from scattering files over your working directory.

recipes.title: Inspect image dimensions
recipes.explanation: Reports format, dimensions and colour depth without modifying the file.

recipes.title: Make a web-sized image
recipes.explanation: Creates a new WebP and removes metadata. The > prevents upscaling. Keep the original file.

recipes.title: Extract text from an image
recipes.explanation: Runs OCR locally, with no upload. Non-English text needs that language's data package installed.

recipes.title: List OCR languages
recipes.explanation: Check what is installed before assuming a language works. Each one is a separate package.

recipes.title: Reach a command an alias is shadowing
recipes.explanation: If gs is an alias for git status, command skips the alias and runs the real executable. whence -va gs shows both.

recipes.title: Hash a downloaded file
recipes.explanation: Compare with the publisher's checksum through a trusted channel. The hash alone does not prove provenance.

recipes.title: Inspect a SQLite database read-only
recipes.explanation: Replace the file path. Read-only mode prevents accidental database writes.

recipes.title: Show SQLite schema
recipes.explanation: Read structure before querying. Do not point this at an unknown production database file.

recipes.title: Check native build tools
recipes.explanation: Many tools compile from source when there is no binary for your platform. Keep build output in a per-project directory.

recipes.title: Find a native library's flags
recipes.explanation: Returns the compiler and linker flags for an installed library. pkgconf provides the pkg-config command on most systems.

recipes.title: Check a Go project
recipes.explanation: Run in a Go module. Tests may execute arbitrary project code and access configured resources.

recipes.title: Inspect Go environment paths
recipes.explanation: Select only needed fields instead of dumping all environment variables.

recipes.title: Check a language server
recipes.explanation: Language servers power editor completion and diagnostics. They normally run through the editor, not by hand.

recipes.title: Inspect a tree-sitter grammar
recipes.explanation: Parser tooling behind modern syntax highlighting. The library and the CLI are separate packages.

recipes.title: Check HTTP headers
recipes.explanation: Sends a HEAD request. Useful for redirects, caching and content type without downloading the page body.

recipes.title: Inspect a local web app
recipes.explanation: Prints the HTTP status code. It fails if no service is listening.

recipes.title: Read a local JSON API
recipes.explanation: Friendly HTTP client. Replace with an endpoint your application actually implements.

recipes.title: Download to an explicit file
recipes.explanation: Example URL must be replaced. --fail makes HTTP errors fail the command; --location follows redirects.

recipes.title: Continue an interrupted download
recipes.explanation: Replace the URL. Resumes if the server supports it and writes into the current directory.

recipes.title: Find a port listener
recipes.explanation: Identify the process holding a port before stopping anything. On Linux, ss -tlnp answers the same question.

recipes.title: See all listening TCP ports
recipes.explanation: -nP skips DNS and service-name lookups, so the output is fast and literal.

recipes.title: Stop a stuck local dev server
recipes.explanation: Sends SIGTERM to every listener on that port. Try Ctrl+C in the owning terminal first; this discards unsaved work in that process.

recipes.title: Look up DNS
recipes.explanation: Shows DNS answers, not an HTTP response. Useful when the browser cannot find a host.

recipes.title: Inspect a TLS handshake
recipes.explanation: Uses SNI for the correct certificate. Check verification output; the handshake alone is not an application health check.

recipes.title: Open the current directory
recipes.explanation: Opens the directory in Finder on macOS. The Linux equivalent is xdg-open .

recipes.title: Copy a file to the clipboard
recipes.explanation: macOS clipboard. Replaces its contents. On Linux use xclip -selection clipboard or wl-copy. Never pipe secrets into a synced clipboard.

recipes.title: Read clipboard text
recipes.explanation: Prints the macOS text clipboard. On Linux use xclip -o -selection clipboard or wl-paste.

recipes.title: Keep a long job awake
recipes.explanation: Prevents idle sleep only while the command runs. Does not permanently change power settings.

recipes.title: Check battery and power source
recipes.explanation: Read-only power status.

recipes.title: Check memory pressure
recipes.explanation: macOS memory statistics. Never use its pressure-generation options for a routine check. On Linux, read free -h and /proc/pressure/memory.

recipes.title: Check swap use
recipes.explanation: Snapshot of swap usage; sustained pressure matters more than a single number.

recipes.title: Inspect CPU and memory interactively
recipes.explanation: Full-screen resource dashboard. q exits. htop is the lighter classic alternative.

recipes.title: Use the macOS process monitor
recipes.explanation: One snapshot sorted by CPU. macOS top flags differ from Linux top.

recipes.title: Inspect processes with procs
recipes.explanation: A more readable ps. macOS permissions limit what any tool can see about other users' processes.

recipes.title: Alternative process dashboard
recipes.explanation: The classic interactive process viewer. F10 or q exits.

recipes.title: Check disk capacity
recipes.explanation: Shows mounted filesystem space in a table. df -h is the built-in alternative.

recipes.title: Find a directory's large children
recipes.explanation: Read-only size scan, two levels deep. Point it at a directory rather than scanning the whole disk.

recipes.title: See macOS version
recipes.explanation: Reports installed macOS version and build.

recipes.title: Inspect hardware
recipes.explanation: macOS hardware summary. It includes serial identifiers: redact them before sharing the output. On Linux use lscpu and free -h.

recipes.title: Check developer tools
recipes.explanation: Prints the active macOS developer-tools directory. Many Homebrew builds need Apple's Command Line Tools.

recipes.title: Review an SSH host config
recipes.explanation: Prints effective SSH configuration for a host alias without connecting. Replace the alias; output may include private network paths.

recipes.title: Preview a directory sync
recipes.explanation: -n is a dry run. A trailing slash on the source copies its contents rather than the directory itself. Read the plan before removing -n.

recipes.title: List GPG public keys
recipes.explanation: Read-only inventory of public keys. Never export secret keys just to debug signing.

recipes.title: Inspect a file type
recipes.explanation: Useful before deciding whether a file is text, binary, an archive or an executable.

recipes.title: Open a project in VS Code
recipes.explanation: Opens the current directory, if the code command is on your PATH. Set EDITOR="code --wait" so Git waits for the window to close.

recipes.title: Open a terminal editor
recipes.explanation: Neovim with no configuration is already usable. Distributions such as LazyVim add language support on top.

recipes.title: Learn Vim interactively
recipes.explanation: Opens Neovim's tutorial. Esc returns to normal mode; :q exits, :w saves.

recipes.title: Start a named session
recipes.explanation: Creates a terminal session that survives terminal disconnection. Default prefix is Ctrl+B.

recipes.title: List sessions
recipes.explanation: Shows saved sessions; no server running is normal if you have never started tmux.

recipes.title: Reattach a session
recipes.explanation: Return to the named dev session. Ctrl+B then D detaches without stopping processes.

recipes.title: Inspect tmux bindings
recipes.explanation: Available once a server exists. Default prefix shortcuts: % split vertically, double quote split horizontally, c new window.

recipes.title: Validate a terminal config
recipes.explanation: Checks the config file for errors before you reload. On macOS the binary lives inside the app bundle: /Applications/Ghostty.app/Contents/MacOS/ghostty.

recipes.title: Read every terminal option
recipes.explanation: Prints the documented defaults for the installed build. Pipe it into less; it is long.

recipes.title: Check direnv state
recipes.explanation: Shows whether this directory's environment is loaded and permitted. direnv needs a hook in your .zshrc to do anything.

recipes.title: Allow a reviewed environment
recipes.explanation: Executes the directory's .envrc as shell code. Read it first, especially in a newly cloned repository.

recipes.title: Get short practical help
recipes.explanation: tealdeer provides the tldr executable. If its cache is missing, tldr --update downloads examples.

recipes.title: Read full help
recipes.explanation: Almost every tool answers --help. Use man for system commands, and SUBCOMMAND --help for nested CLIs such as git or docker.

recipes.title: Inspect a package
recipes.explanation: Shows version, description, dependencies and installation details. Package name ripgrep provides executable rg.

recipes.title: List installed command packages
recipes.explanation: Includes libraries and transitive dependencies, not just user-facing CLIs.

recipes.title: List installed desktop packages
recipes.explanation: macOS GUI apps and fonts installed through Homebrew. Fonts provide no commands of their own.

recipes.title: Understand why a library exists
recipes.explanation: Shows installed packages that depend on libpng. Avoid manually deleting dependency directories.

recipes.title: List leaf packages
recipes.explanation: Packages not required by other installed formulae. A leaf is not necessarily unused.

recipes.title: Check missing dependencies
recipes.explanation: No output is the good result: every installed formula has what it declares.

recipes.title: Run Homebrew diagnostics
recipes.explanation: Reports common installation problems. Read each warning before acting; never answer a permissions warning with a recursive sudo chown.

recipes.title: Refresh package metadata
recipes.explanation: Downloads current metadata; does not upgrade all installed formulae.

recipes.title: Review available updates
recipes.explanation: Run after brew update. Read the list before upgrading; a major version bump can change a tool's flags.

recipes.title: Upgrade one selected tool
recipes.explanation: Updates only the selected formula and any needed dependencies. Verify your workflow after upgrading.

recipes.title: Preview cache cleanup
recipes.explanation: Lists what would be removed without deleting anything. Drop --dry-run only after reading the list.

recipes.title: Preview unused dependency removal
recipes.explanation: Read the proposed list before considering a real removal.

recipes.title: Locate a package's files
recipes.explanation: Lists files installed by a package, including executables that may not be linked into PATH.

recipes.title: Export a reproducible package list
recipes.explanation: Writes a Brewfile listing what you installed. It refuses to overwrite an existing file unless forced. This is how you rebuild a machine.

recipes.title: Check a Brewfile
recipes.explanation: Compares a manifest with installed dependencies. It does not install missing packages.

recipes.title: Inspect a cask
recipes.explanation: Shows a GUI app's version, install path and upstream site. Casks are macOS-only.

recipes.title: Update an isolated Python tool
recipes.explanation: Upgrades that tool's own environment and nothing else. Replace ruff with a tool from uv tool list.

recipes.title: See local pnpm storage
recipes.explanation: Prints the shared content-addressed store location. Do not delete it while installs run.

recipes.title: Check Git settings with origins
recipes.explanation: Shows which file each setting came from. A narrow pattern avoids dumping credentials and private remote URLs.

recipes.title: Read a file without decorations
recipes.explanation: Plain text is best for pipelines and scripts; bat is useful for interactive reading.

recipes.title: Read the beginning of a log
recipes.explanation: Replace the example filename. Avoid printing entire large logs or files containing secrets.

recipes.title: Follow a rotating log
recipes.explanation: Follows the filename across replacement or rotation. Ctrl+C stops watching.

recipes.title: Extract a range of lines
recipes.explanation: Prints a line range without editing the file. macOS ships BSD sed, Linux ships GNU sed, and their in-place editing flags differ.

recipes.title: Count lines, words and bytes
recipes.explanation: Reports basic text counts. wc -l selects lines; wc -c selects bytes.

recipes.title: Sort and deduplicate text
recipes.command: printf '%s\n' beta alpha beta | sort | uniq -c
recipes.explanation: Produces a sorted frequency table. uniq only combines adjacent duplicate lines, so sorting matters.

recipes.title: Select a delimited column
recipes.explanation: Works for simple delimiter-separated text. Quoted CSV fields need a proper CSV parser, not cut.

recipes.title: Compute with awk
recipes.explanation: Accumulates the second whitespace-separated field. Start with small sample input to understand the transformation.

recipes.title: Pass filenames without splitting spaces
recipes.explanation: NUL-delimited records preserve spaces and most unusual filenames. This example only prints a preview.

recipes.title: Compare two files
recipes.explanation: Unified diff. Exit 1 means files differ; it is not necessarily a tool failure.

recipes.title: Read long output in a pager
recipes.explanation: Space scrolls a page, / searches, n advances and q quits.

recipes.title: Inspect file permissions
recipes.explanation: Shows mode, owner, group and name. This is BSD syntax for macOS; GNU stat on Linux uses stat -c '%A %U %G %n'.

recipes.title: Understand an executable permission
recipes.explanation: Inspect before changing modes. chmod u+x script.zsh adds execute permission for the owner only.

recipes.title: Search with Spotlight
recipes.explanation: Uses the Spotlight index, so an empty result is not proof a file is absent. fd reads the directory itself.

recipes.title: Inspect mounted disks
recipes.explanation: Lists disks and partitions without modifying them. Disk erase and repair subcommands are separate operations.

recipes.title: Inspect network interfaces
recipes.explanation: Maps hardware ports to device names such as en0. Does not change network configuration.

recipes.title: Inspect macOS DNS configuration
recipes.explanation: Useful when VPN or split DNS behaves differently from a direct dig query. Output can reveal internal network names.

recipes.title: Inspect proxy configuration
recipes.explanation: Read-only check for system HTTP/SOCKS proxy settings. Individual CLI tools may also use environment variables.

recipes.title: Check one preference domain
recipes.explanation: Reads a single Finder preference. A missing key means there is no explicit user override.

recipes.title: Validate a property list
recipes.explanation: Checks plist syntax only. Valid XML does not mean the program it points at will start.

recipes.title: Inspect a launch agent
recipes.explanation: Reports registration and last-exit status for a per-user agent. The Linux equivalent is systemctl --user status.

recipes.title: Check update availability
recipes.explanation: Contacts Apple's update service and lists available updates without installing them. May take a while.

recipes.title: Create a screenshot file
recipes.explanation: Opens macOS interactive capture and writes your selection. Review the visible content before sharing the image.

recipes.title: Show recent app log events
recipes.explanation: Narrows the macOS unified log to one process and a short window. Logs can contain private content. journalctl is the Linux counterpart.

recipes.title: Check backup status
recipes.explanation: Reports Time Machine's current operation. An idle result does not prove a recent backup exists.

recipes.title: Read archive contents
recipes.explanation: Lists what an archive holds without extracting it. Always look before extracting an archive you did not create.

recipes.title: Create a project-note archive
recipes.explanation: Writes an archive from explicit files and folders. Choose a new output path and exclude secrets.

recipes.title: Connect using SSH
recipes.explanation: Replace with your account and host. Verify a new host's fingerprint through a trusted channel before accepting it.

recipes.title: Copy one file over SSH
recipes.explanation: Replace the example user, host and directory. Uploads the file to that host and may overwrite an existing destination file.

recipes.title: Check the selected editor
recipes.explanation: Git and other tools open this. A value such as code --wait makes them wait for the window to close.

recipes.title: Identify the distribution
recipes.explanation: Tells you which package manager and package names apply. Scripts should read ID and VERSION_ID rather than guessing.

recipes.title: See listening ports
recipes.explanation: The Linux answer to lsof for ports. Process names for other users' processes need sudo.

recipes.title: Check a service
recipes.explanation: Shows whether a service is enabled, running and what it last logged. Replace docker with any unit name.

recipes.title: Start a service now and at boot
recipes.explanation: Two things at once: start it, and start it on every boot. Use disable --now to undo both.

recipes.title: Read a service's logs
recipes.explanation: The last 100 lines for one unit. Add -f to follow. Add --since '10 min ago' to bound it by time.

recipes.title: Read your own user services
recipes.explanation: Per-user services, the counterpart to macOS launch agents.

recipes.title: Check memory and swap
recipes.explanation: Human-readable totals. The available column matters more than free: Linux deliberately uses spare memory for cache.

recipes.title: Check memory pressure
recipes.explanation: Pressure stall information: how much time tasks spent waiting on memory. Better evidence than a single free number.

recipes.title: Describe the CPU
recipes.command: lscpu | Cores, threads, architecture and flags. lscpu
recipes.explanation: rg 'Model name' narrows it to one line.

recipes.title: Check disk space
recipes.explanation: Built-in and always present. duf prints the same data in a friendlier table.

recipes.title: Search installed packages
recipes.explanation: Debian and Ubuntu. Fedora uses dnf list installed; Arch uses pacman -Q.

recipes.title: Find which package owns a file
recipes.explanation: Debian and Ubuntu. Fedora uses dnf provides; Arch uses pacman -Qo.

recipes.title: Read a package's description
recipes.explanation: Version, size, dependencies and homepage, before installing anything.

recipes.title: Refresh and inspect updates
recipes.explanation: update refreshes metadata only. Nothing is upgraded until you run apt upgrade.

recipes.title: Make zsh your login shell
recipes.explanation: Takes effect at your next login, not in this terminal. Install zsh first or you will be locked out of a working shell.

recipes.title: Copy to the clipboard
recipes.explanation: X11. On Wayland use wl-copy. macOS uses pbcopy.

recipes.title: Open a file with the desktop default
recipes.explanation: The Linux counterpart to macOS open. Needs a desktop session.

recipes.title: Check your kernel
recipes.explanation: Kernel name, release and machine architecture. Some tools ship separate arm64 and x86_64 builds.

recipes.title: Inspect a user's groups
recipes.explanation: Shows your groups. Running Docker without sudo requires membership in the docker group, which is equivalent to root access.

shortcuts: Move to start / end of command
Cut previous word / paste cut text
Find and insert a file path (fzf)
Search history using your current input
Accept autosuggestion when at the end of input
Complete a command or navigate completion choices
Normal mode → save / quit / save and quit

workflows.title: A deliberate start to a coding session
workflows.intro: Establish context before changing anything. Tools become far more predictable once the directory, branch and runtime are explicit rather than assumed.
workflows.finish: Open a second split or tab for Git and tests. Keep the dev server visible so you notice failures when they happen, not ten minutes later.

workflows.title: Diagnose “port 3000 is already in use”
workflows.intro: Find the owner before killing anything. A port conflict is often an old dev server, but it can just as easily be a different project you still need. On Linux, ss -tlnp replaces lsof.
workflows.finish: Replace PID with the real number. Prefer Ctrl+C in the terminal that owns the server. kill sends SIGTERM, which asks a process to stop and discards its unsaved work.

workflows.title: Bring up and inspect a WordPress site
workflows.intro: Run WordPress through the project’s containers so PHP, WordPress and the database versions stay aligned. This assumes the stack defines a wpcli service.
steps:
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps

docker compose exec wpcli wp core version
docker compose exec wpcli wp plugin list
workflows.finish: Ctrl+C exits logs. docker compose stop preserves the containers and volumes. Database export files are sensitive and should stay out of Git.

workflows.title: Review a change like a senior engineer
workflows.intro: Review behavior, boundaries and failure modes. Commit only changes you can explain.
steps:
git status --short
git diff --stat
git diff
workflows.finish: Run the relevant test script where it exists. A formatter or passing test suite alone does not prove the change solves the right problem.

workflows.title: Switch from web development to local AI
workflows.intro: A language model, a container VM and a browser all want the same RAM. On a 16–24 GB machine you have to choose between them rather than run everything.
steps: Stop the container VM if you no longer need it
Restore the VM when you need it again
workflows.finish: Stopping the VM interrupts every container, so finish their work first. If memory is tight, choose a smaller model or a shorter context. A model’s file size is a floor for its memory use, not a measurement of it. On Linux, replace the colima steps with systemctl start/stop docker.

workflows.title: Maintain packages without surprise upgrades
workflows.intro: Refresh metadata, read the proposed changes, then upgrade deliberately. Dependency libraries are part of the toolchain, not clutter to be pruned. Homebrew here; apt, dnf and pacman have the same three phases.
workflows.finish: Never answer a permissions warning with a recursive sudo chown on a package directory. Upgrade one tool at a time when a project depends on its behaviour, and read release notes for anything that crosses a major version.

workflows.title: Turn a one-off command into reliable automation
workflows.intro: Start with a read-only preview, understand filenames and exit codes, then write the smallest script that does the job. ShellCheck targets sh and bash; zsh -n is the syntax check for zsh scripts.
steps: for file in *.txt(N); do print -r -- "$file"; done
Check a zsh script before running it
workflows.finish: Quote variable expansions, use -- before user-provided paths, check failures, and never parse ls output. For filename pipelines use null separators, such as fd -0 with xargs -0, and preview the action first.

lessons: Use pwd, cd, z, ll, fd and Ctrl+R without guessing where you are.
Find a source file in one project, preview it with bat, then return with cd -.
Understand command, subcommand, flags, arguments, quotes and exit status.
Use stdout, stderr, pipes, command substitution and redirection intentionally.
Count tracked TypeScript files with git ls-files and wc; explain why node_modules is excluded.
Use dry-runs, diffs, explicit paths and narrow queries.
Stage two separate hunks with git add -p and inspect git diff --staged.
Check directory, executable, runtime, environment, port, logs and resource pressure.
Diagnose a failed dev-server start using whence -va, lsof and the project log.
Understand which layer owns what: the system package manager, the runtime manager, the project manager and containers.
Explain which layer owns Node, React, Python, PHP and WordPress on your machine, and what breaks if two layers install the same thing.
Write small scripts, check exits, preserve backups, use worktrees and document operations.
Create a read-only project-health script and test it in a directory whose name contains spaces.
Compare real workloads, change one thing at a time, and be honest about what a measurement proves.
Use hyperfine on two harmless searches, then explain what the result does and does not prove.

tools.name: zsh
tools.description: The shell every example in this handbook is written for.
tools.note: Default on macOS since Catalina. On Linux, install it and then run chsh -s "$(command -v zsh)" to make it your login shell.

tools.name: zsh-autosuggestions
tools.description: Suggests the rest of a command from your history as you type.
tools.note: A plugin, not a command. It has to be sourced from your .zshrc; the package description prints the path to source.

tools.name: zsh-syntax-highlighting
tools.description: Colours a command line as valid or invalid before you press Enter.
tools.note: Source it last in your .zshrc, after every other plugin, or it will not see later keybindings.

tools.name: direnv
tools.description: Loads and unloads environment variables when you enter or leave a directory.
tools.note: Needs a shell hook in your .zshrc. It executes .envrc files, so only allow them in repositories you trust.

tools.name: fzf
tools.description: Fuzzy finder. Provides Ctrl+R history search and Ctrl+T file search.
tools.note: The key bindings are a separate setup step; see the project README for the line to add to your .zshrc.

tools.name: zoxide
tools.description: Directory jumper that learns where you actually work. Provides z and zi.
tools.note: Needs eval "$(zoxide init zsh)" in your .zshrc. Older Debian and Ubuntu releases ship a version without zi.

tools.name: fd
tools.description: Fast, sensible file finder. A friendlier front end than find.
tools.note: On Debian and Ubuntu the binary is installed as fdfind; alias fd=fdfind or symlink it.

tools.name: ripgrep
tools.description: Fast recursive content search that respects .gitignore.

tools.name: eza
tools.description: Modern ls replacement with colours, icons, tree view and Git status.
tools.note: Not in older Debian and Ubuntu archives; the project documents an apt repository for those releases.

tools.name: bat
tools.description: cat with syntax highlighting, line numbers and paging.
tools.note: On Debian and Ubuntu the binary is installed as batcat; alias bat=batcat or symlink it.

tools.name: tree
tools.description: Prints a directory as an indented tree.

tools.name: glow
tools.description: Renders Markdown readably in the terminal.
tools.note: Packaged on Arch and Fedora; on Debian and Ubuntu use the Charm apt repository or a release binary.

tools.name: tealdeer
tools.description: Fast client for tldr, the community cheat sheets. Provides tldr.
tools.note: Run tldr --update once after installing to fetch the page cache.

tools.name: jq
tools.description: Query and reshape JSON on the command line.

tools.name: yq
tools.description: The same idea as jq, for YAML, TOML and XML.
tools.note: Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora package a different, Python-based yq. For the Go yq used here, install the release binary from the project page.

tools.name: jless
tools.description: Pager for large JSON documents. Fold, search and navigate instead of scrolling.
tools.note: Not packaged on Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora; install with cargo install jless or a release binary.

tools.name: sd
tools.description: Find and replace with plain syntax. An easier sed for simple substitutions.
tools.note: sd rewrites files in place. Preview with ripgrep first; it has no undo.

tools.name: tokei
tools.description: Counts lines of code by language.

tools.name: git
tools.description: Version control. The handbook assumes a recent version.
tools.note: macOS ships an Xcode version of Git. Installing it via Homebrew keeps it current.

tools.name: gh
tools.description: GitHub from the terminal: pull requests, issues, releases, CI runs.
tools.note: Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora need the GitHub apt/dnf repository first; the manual documents the exact steps.

tools.name: git-delta
tools.description: Readable, syntax-highlighted diffs for git diff and git log.
tools.note: Configure it as your pager in .gitconfig; installing alone changes nothing.

tools.name: git-lfs
tools.description: Stores large binary files outside the Git history.
tools.note: Run git lfs install once per machine after installing.

tools.name: lazygit
tools.description: Full-screen Git interface for staging hunks and reading history.
tools.note: Not in the Debian or Ubuntu archives; use the release binary from the project page.

tools.name: btop
tools.description: Resource monitor for CPU, memory, disks, network and processes.

tools.name: htop
tools.description: The classic interactive process viewer.

tools.name: procs
tools.description: ps with readable columns, colour and search.

tools.name: dust
tools.description: Shows which directories are actually using your disk.
tools.note: The Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora package is named du-dust; the binary is still dust.

tools.name: duf
tools.description: Readable df: free space per filesystem.

tools.name: lsof
tools.description: Lists open files and sockets. How you find what is holding a port.
tools.note: Already present on macOS. On Linux, ss -tlnp from iproute2 answers the same port question and is usually installed.

tools.name: hyperfine
tools.description: Benchmarks commands with warmup runs and statistics.

tools.name: watchexec
tools.description: Re-runs a command when files change.
tools.note: Not in the Debian or Ubuntu archives; use cargo install watchexec-cli or a release binary.

tools.name: trash
tools.description: Deletes to the desktop trash instead of unlinking. A safer rm for interactive use.
tools.note: These are two different projects with the same idea. On Linux the command is usually trash-put.

tools.name: curl
tools.description: Transfers data over HTTP and many other protocols.

tools.name: wget
tools.description: Downloads files, including recursive mirroring.

tools.name: xh
tools.description: Friendly HTTP client for testing APIs. Prints headers and JSON readably.
tools.note: Not in the Debian or Ubuntu archives; use the release binary from the project page.

tools.name: neovim
tools.description: The editor the handbook assumes when it says "open the file".
tools.note: Distribution packages lag upstream. If a plugin requires a newer Neovim, use the official AppImage or release archive.

tools.name: tmux
tools.description: Keeps shell sessions alive across disconnects and splits one terminal into panes.

tools.name: uv
tools.description: Installs Python versions, manages project environments and runs isolated CLI tools.
tools.note: On Debian, Ubuntu and older Fedora, use the official installer at https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh after reading it.

tools.name: volta
tools.description: Pins a Node and package-manager version per project, then switches automatically.
tools.note: On Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora, use the installer at https://get.volta.sh. Volta then installs Node itself: volta install node@22.

tools.name: go
tools.description: The Go toolchain. Needed to build some of the tools listed here from source.

tools.name: docker
tools.description: Builds and runs containers. Provides docker and docker compose.
tools.note: On Linux the engine runs natively; enable it with sudo systemctl enable --now docker and add yourself to the docker group. On macOS the CLI needs a VM: see colima. Docker's own repository usually carries a newer engine than the distribution package.

tools.name: docker-compose
tools.description: Runs multi-container projects from a compose.yaml file.
tools.note: This is the v2 plugin invoked as docker compose, with a space. The old docker-compose script is a separate, retired project.

tools.name: colima
tools.description: Runs the Linux VM that Docker needs on macOS. macOS only.
tools.note: macOS only, and not needed on Linux, where containers run on the host kernel. An alternative to Docker Desktop.

tools.name: lazydocker
tools.description: Full-screen view of containers, logs and resource use.
tools.note: Not in the Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora archives; use the release binary from the project page.

tools.name: dive
tools.description: Inspects an image layer by layer to find what is making it large.
tools.note: Not in the Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora archives; the project publishes .deb and .rpm packages.

tools.name: hadolint
tools.description: Lints Dockerfiles for common mistakes.
tools.note: Packaged on Arch via the AUR; elsewhere use the release binary from the project page.

tools.name: kubernetes-cli
tools.description: Talks to a Kubernetes cluster. Provides kubectl.
tools.note: Debian and Ubuntu need the Kubernetes apt repository first; the documentation covers the steps.

tools.name: k9s
tools.description: Full-screen Kubernetes browser for pods, logs and events.
tools.note: Not in the Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora archives; use the release binary from the project page.

tools.name: helm
tools.description: Installs and upgrades packaged Kubernetes applications.
tools.note: Debian and Ubuntu need the Helm apt repository; the documentation covers the steps.

tools.name: ollama
tools.description: Downloads and runs language models locally.
tools.note: On Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora, use the installer at https://ollama.com/install.sh after reading it. Models are large: check disk space first, and expect memory use in the same order as the model file.

tools.name: llama.cpp
tools.description: Runs GGUF models directly. Provides llama-cli and llama-server.
tools.note: Most Linux users build it from source to match their GPU; the repository documents the build flags.

tools.name: imagemagick
tools.description: Converts, resizes and inspects images. Provides magick.

tools.name: ghostscript
tools.description: Processes PostScript and PDF. Provides gs.
tools.note: If you alias gs to git status, the alias wins. Call the full path to reach Ghostscript.

tools.name: tesseract
tools.description: Extracts text from images (OCR).
tools.note: Each language is a separate data package, for example tesseract-ocr-deu on Debian and Ubuntu.

extras: Ghostty, WezTerm, Kitty and Alacritty are all GPU-accelerated and cross-platform. macOS Terminal, GNOME Console and Konsole run every command here too.
Only needed if you want icons in a prompt or file listing. JetBrainsMono Nerd Font is a safe default. Install it, then select it in your terminal settings.
Starship and Oh My Posh both show Git state, runtime versions and exit status. Entirely optional: the handbook never depends on your prompt.
